canonical_statement: The study evaluated whether cardiometabolic index (CMI) was associated with all-cause and cardiovascular mortality among adults aged 20–65 years with diabetes in NHANES.
The analytic cohort included 2,188 NHANES 1999–2018 participants aged 20–65 years with diabetes and complete CMI, follow-up, and covariate data.

population.label: NHANES 1999–2018 participants aged 20–65 years with diabetes and complete follow-up/covariate data
inclusion_criteria: Diabetes by laboratory criteria, self-report, or glucose-lowering medication use

canonical_statement: Diabetes was defined by fasting plasma glucose ≥126 mg/dL, HbA1c ≥6.5%, 2-hour OGTT glucose ≥200 mg/dL, self-reported diagnosis, or use of insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents.

population.label: Diabetes eligibility definition
inclusion_criteria: FPG ≥126 mg/dL or HbA1c ≥6.5% or 2-hour OGTT glucose ≥200 mg/dL or self-reported diabetes or insulin/oral hypoglycemic use

canonical_statement: The source was a population-based observational cohort analysis using NHANES 1999–2018 with mortality follow-up through December 31, 2019.
Participant flow reduced 101,316 NHANES records to 2,188 analytic participants after age restriction, missing CMI exclusion, diabetes selection, and complete-case follow-up/covariate exclusion.
All-cause mortality was identified by probabilistic linkage of NHANES records to the National Death Index with supplementary mortality surveillance sources.

outcome.definition: Mortality identified through NHANES linkage to the National Death Index and supplementary mortality sources

canonical_statement: Cardiovascular mortality was cause-classified using the manuscript’s listed ICD-10 codes I00-I09, I11, I13, and I20-I51, with follow-up ending December 31, 2019.

outcome.definition: Cause-specific mortality described using ICD-10 codes I00-I09, I11, I13, and I20-I51 in the manuscript
outcome.measurement_method: Mortality linkage and ICD-10 cause coding

canonical_statement: CMI was calculated as (triglycerides/HDL-C) multiplied by waist-to-height ratio and treated as the study exposure.
The dichotomous CMI cutoff was 1.84 and was selected with maximally selected rank statistics for the strongest survival association.
Analyses incorporated NHANES sample weights, clustering, and stratification to account for the complex survey design.

Cox models were fit as unadjusted Model 1, age/sex/race-adjusted Model 2, and Model 3 additionally adjusted for education, smoking, drinking, weight, total cholesterol, eGFR, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease.
The analysis also used Kaplan–Meier/log-rank methods, restricted cubic splines, stratified interaction analyses, Spearman correlations, ROC/AUC comparisons, and DeLong tests.
At the 1.84 cutoff, 366 participants were in the higher-CMI group and 1,822 were in the lower-CMI group.

population.label: CMI-stratified analytic cohort

canonical_statement: Compared with the lower-CMI group, the higher-CMI group had higher BMI, waist circumference, WHtR, total cholesterol, triglycerides, HbA1c, and fasting glucose, and lower HDL-C.

canonical_statement: The authors concluded that higher CMI was associated with greater all-cause and cardiovascular mortality and could serve as a long-term prognostic indicator in this population.
The authors proposed CMI as a simple, non-invasive risk-stratification metric derived from commonly measured clinical parameters.
The authors acknowledged residual or unmeasured confounding despite multivariable adjustment.
The authors acknowledged that the observational cohort design does not establish causality.
The authors reported receiving no specific funding for the work.
The authors declared no competing interests.
The authors stated that all data used in the study are available from the NHANES database.
